screens.title: Resolving Disk Space and Storage-Related Problems
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter teaches you how to find where PostgreSQL consumes disk space, why storage grows beyond live data, and how to fix it with practical maintenance. You will learn the pg_* size functions that give precise disk measurements, the causes and costs of table and index bloat, and the operational choices between VACUUM and VACUUM FULL. We'll also cover autovacuum tuning so vacuuming keeps pace with updates, how to identify costly temporary-file spill behavior tied to work_mem, and the critical problem of transaction ID wraparound and how to monitor and prevent it. By the end, you'll be able to run targeted queries to list large relations, interpret n_dead_tup and pg_total_relation_size, and choose maintenance steps that minimize downtime. A quick example: you will see how a table with heavy updates can report millions of dead tuples while still serving queries; a careful VACUUM reclaims reuse capacity while VACUUM FULL returns space to the OS but requires an exclusive lock. Think about a busy log or audit table: do you vacuum frequently to avoid massive bloat, or schedule a maintenance window for VACUUM FULL if you must release disk to the operating system? That contrast will guide many operational choices in real systems.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Resolving Disk Space
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Resolving Disk Space and Storage-Related Problems

Measure usage with pg_* functions, diagnose table and index bloat, tune autovacuum, and choose safe reclaim strategies.

In this lesson

You will identify large relations, observe bloat impact, run VACUUM and VACUUM FULL, tune autovacuum, and monitor XID age to avoid wraparound.

Why it matters

Unchecked storage growth can slow queries, increase I/O, and cause outages if disks fill or transaction IDs approach wraparound thresholds.

Explore Key Topics
Measuring usage
Use pg_relation_size, pg_total_relation_size, and pg_database_size to find space hot spots.
Bloat & Vacuum
Understand dead tuples, VACUUM vs VACUUM FULL, and autovacuum tuning to control growth.
XID & Temp files
Monitor transaction ID age and temporary-file spills from low work_mem to avoid corruption and slow queries.
Storage map
Quick visual
Database
pg_database_size shows total footprint.
Relation
pg_relation_size and pg_total_relation_size separate table and index usage.
Bloat
Dead tuples inflate on-disk size; VACUUM reclaims reuse space.
XID risk
Monitor datfrozenxid/relfrozenxid to avoid wraparound.

screens.narratorSegment: Over the next screens you will gain measurable skills that let you find where PostgreSQL stores data, identify waste, and take safe corrective action. First, you will be able to identify and quantify disk usage by databases, tables, and indexes using the pg_database_size, pg_relation_size and related functions. That skill helps you map storage consumption and prioritize targets. Second, you will learn to recognize table and index bloat, what causes it under MVCC, and how bloat affects input and output and cache efficiency. Third, you will become fluent with VACUUM strategies: when to run a regular VACUUM, when VACUUM FULL is appropriate, and how autovacuum settings influence system behavior. Finally, you will monitor temporary-file creation and transaction ID age to prevent performance issues and critical wraparound risks. Each objective includes small, practical checks you can run immediately, so these are not just concepts — they are operational tasks you can perform to keep production systems healthy.

screens.title: Inspecting disk usage with pg_* functions
screens.narratorSegment: A necessary first step in any storage problem is measurement. PostgreSQL provides a small set of functions that let you measure database, tablespace, relation, and index usage precisely. For example, pg_database_size returns the total size of a database on disk. Pg_relation_size returns the size of a table's data fork only, while pg_total_relation_size includes indexes and TOAST. Pg_indexes_size reports the combined size of all indexes for a table. These functions are safe to run and are efficient ways to focus your attention on the largest consumers. A common pattern is to query pg_class or pg_stat_user_tables and order by pg_total_relation_size to list the top space users; that is the practical starting point for most cleanup tasks. A frequent misconception is to assume that VACUUM will always reduce the number reported by pg_total_relation_size; regular VACUUM frees tuples for reuse inside the same file but does not shrink the file on disk. Only VACUUM FULL, which rewrites the table, returns space to the operating system. As an example, run a size query before and after running VACUUM to confirm whether your goal is reuse within the table or returning space to the OS. Key takeaway: measure first, then decide whether reuse or return to OS is the goal.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Inspecting disk usage
Definition

pg_* size functions return on-disk sizes. Use them to separate table data, index size, and total relation footprint before taking action.

Quick reference
  • pg_database_size(name) — total bytes for a database.
  • pg_relation_size(oid) — table data fork size (no indexes).
  • pg_total_relation_size(oid) — table plus indexes and TOAST.
  • pg_indexes_size(oid) — combined index size for a table.
Key Takeaway

Always capture sizes before and after maintenance to prove the action you chose actually met the operational goal.

Example query
-- Check database sizes
SELECT datname, pg_size_pretty(pg_database_size(datname))
FROM pg_database
ORDER BY pg_database_size(datname) DESC;

-- Relation-level sizes
SELECT relname,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(oid)) AS total_size,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(oid)) AS table_size,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size(oid)) AS indexes_size
FROM pg_class
WHERE relkind = 'r'
ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(oid) DESC
LIMIT 20;
Common mistake

Expecting pg_total_relation_size to immediately shrink after a regular VACUUM. VACUUM frees space for reuse in the table file but does not reduce the on-disk file size unless you run VACUUM FULL.

screens.title: Finding the largest tables and indexes
screens.narratorSegment: When disk usage is high you need to prioritize. The provided SELECT using pg_class and pg_total_relation_size gives a ranked list of relations by total on-disk footprint. This is practical because it shows both the table data and indexes, letting you spot tables where indexes dominate or vice versa. The query also returns human-friendly sizes so you can quickly share results with stakeholders. A concrete example: if you find a table with a large index footprint but few live tuples, index bloat is likely. Conversely, a table with a huge table_size and few dead tuples may simply hold a lot of live data. A common misconception is to assume the largest tables are always the best candidates for VACUUM FULL; instead, start by inspecting n_dead_tup and recent update patterns. Use the code here to run in a staging environment, capture results, and annotate which relations need further investigation. Closing question: after you list the top twenty relations, which two would you investigate first and why? Finding the largest tables and indexes means use pg_total_relation_size to create an ordered list of targets and then inspect live/dead tuple counts to decide actions.. In practical terms, a practical query to prioritize cleanup targets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Largest tables query
Title

Identify the biggest on-disk relations so you can focus maintenance where it matters most.

Interpretation checklist
  • If indexes are large relative to table data, consider index-only maintenance or reindexing.
  • If n_dead_tup is high, plan a VACUUM; if space must be returned to OS, plan VACUUM FULL during a window.
  • Look for skew: a few relations often consume the majority of disk space.
Check your understanding

After running the query, inspect n_dead_tup and recent update patterns for the top two relations before choosing VACUUM or VACUUM FULL.

Recommended query
SELECT
    relname AS "Table",
    pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(oid)) AS "Total Size",
    pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(oid)) AS "Table Size",
    pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size(oid)) AS "Indexes Size",
    n_live_tup AS "Live Tuples",
    n_dead_tup AS "Dead Tuples"
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(oid) DESC
LIMIT 20;
Concrete example

If a table shows Total Size 50 GB, Table Size 5 GB, and Indexes Size 45 GB with few live tuples, focus on index bloat or unnecessary indexes rather than table data.

screens.title: Table bloat: what it is and why it happens
screens.narratorSegment: Table bloat arises from PostgreSQL's MVCC model where updates and deletes create new row versions and mark old ones as dead. Those dead tuples remain in the table until VACUUM marks their space reusable. If updates or deletes are frequent and vacuuming is too slow, the on-disk file grows with many dead tuples. That causes larger reads, increased input and output, slower sequential scans, and reduced cache efficiency. An example: a table with one million live rows but five million dead tuples will require scanning many pages containing dead data, harming performance and increasing storage usage. Important nuance: a regular VACUUM reclaims space for reuse inside the table file so future inserts can use that free space, but it does not shrink the file visible to the operating system. VACUUM FULL rewrites the table to a smaller file and returns the freed space to the OS, but it locks the table and is therefore a maintenance-window operation. A common misconception is to equate a lower n_dead_tup with no bloat; sometimes n_dead_tup can be reset by VACUUM while the file remains large because vacuum did not shrink the file. Closing takeaway: measure live and dead tuples, decide whether reuse or OS-level shrinkage is the goal, and then choose VACUUM or VACUUM FULL accordingly.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Table bloat
What causes it

Under MVCC, UPDATE and DELETE create dead tuples. If VACUUM can't keep up, dead tuples accumulate and the physical file grows.

Consequences
  • Higher disk usage and I/O when scanning tables.
  • Worse cache efficiency in shared buffers.
  • Longer sequential and index scans.
Misconception check

A drop in n_dead_tup after VACUUM does not necessarily mean the file shrank. Use pg_total_relation_size to confirm whether space was returned to the OS.

Detecting bloat

Use pg_stat_user_tables to read n_live_tup and n_dead_tup and combine with pg_total_relation_size to estimate bloat ratio using community bloat queries.

Concrete example

If n_live_tup = 1,000,000 and n_dead_tup = 5,000,000, the table likely has heavy bloat and will benefit from immediate vacuuming. Decide whether VACUUM or VACUUM FULL is appropriate based on whether you must return space to the OS.

screens.title: Index bloat and its effects
screens.narratorSegment: Index bloat occurs when indexed columns are frequently updated, and the index retains dead entries that are no longer needed. For B-tree indexes, this increases tree height and page count and leads to larger index scans and more random input and output. Index bloat may be less visible in pg_relation_size because index space is reported separately, but pg_indexes_size and pg_total_relation_size will reveal large index footprints. A concrete example is a heavily updated timestamp column that is part of many indexes; repeated updates generate dead index entries that remain until reindexing or maintenance collapses them. Misconceptions include thinking that VACUUM always fixes index bloat; while VACUUM can clean some index entries, heavy index bloat often requires REINDEX or even index drop-and-recreate to reclaim space effectively. When inspecting a large index, consider whether the index is needed or whether it can be rebuilt during a maintenance window. Key takeaway: treat index bloat separately from table bloat and choose reindexing if index pages are the primary consumer of disk and performance is suffering. Index bloat and its effects means large indexes slow lookups; consider reindex or index rebuilds when vacuum is insufficient.. In practical terms, how index dead entries harm lookups and what to do about them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Index bloat
Why index bloat happens

Updates to indexed columns leave old index entries behind. Over time, these entries make the index larger and scans slower.

Detection steps
  • Compare pg_indexes_size with expected index sizes.
  • Check index page counts and depth; increased depth often correlates with bloat.
  • Use community bloat queries that estimate ideal index size.
Pro tip

If index bloat is the problem, REINDEX or drop-and-create during a maintenance window often yields the best space recovery with reduced complexity versus VACUUM FULL.

Concrete scenario

A table with heavy updates on a column used in three indexes shows high pg_indexes_size. Reindex one heavy index at a time to reduce impact and monitor query plans for improvement.

Common mistake

Assuming VACUUM will always reduce index size. In many cases, vacuuming lowers dead entries but does not compact the index file; reindexing is needed to shrink the on-disk index footprint.

screens.title: VACUUM, VACUUM FULL, and practical steps
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding between VACUUM and VACUUM FULL is a matter of goals and availability. VACUUM reclaims space occupied by dead tuples and marks it for reuse within the same table file. It is safe to run concurrently and typically should be the first step to reduce n_dead_tup and improve future operations. VACUUM FULL rewrites the table and its indexes to new files, physically shrinking the on-disk footprint and returning space to the operating system; however, it requires an exclusive lock and can block concurrent access, so schedule it during a maintenance window. A safe operational flow is: 1) Measure sizes and dead tuples; 2) Run VACUUM to reclaim reuse space and reduce dead tuple counts; 3) If you must return space to the OS for capacity reasons, plan VACUUM FULL during a quiet period and inform stakeholders. Misconception: running VACUUM FULL repeatedly without addressing root causes such as high update churn or insufficient autovacuum will only delay recurrence. Example commands shown here include VACUUM VERBOSE my_table and VACUUM FULL VERBOSE my_table. Closing question: for a busy audit table with five times more dead tuples than live tuples, which vacuum do you run first and why?

keyIdea.title: Choose VACUUM by goal
keyIdea.text: VACUUM reclaims reuse within the file and is non-blocking; VACUUM FULL returns space to OS but is blocking and should be used sparingly.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › VACUUM strategies
Step-by-step
  1. Measure relation sizes and dead tuple counts.
  2. Run VACUUM VERBOSE to reclaim space for reuse and update stats.
  3. If disk must be shrunk, schedule VACUUM FULL during a maintenance window.
  4. Monitor and tune autovacuum to prevent recurrence.
Commands
-- Non-blocking: reclaims space for reuse
VACUUM VERBOSE my_table;

-- Blocking: rewrites and returns space to OS
VACUUM FULL VERBOSE my_table;
Common-mistake

Running VACUUM FULL repeatedly without addressing autovacuum tuning or update patterns will cause recurring bloat and repeated blocking operations.

Concrete example

Start with VACUUM VERBOSE on an audit_logs table with many dead tuples to reduce n_dead_tup and improve reuse. If you must free disk immediately, plan VACUUM FULL in a maintenance window.

Key takeaway

VACUUM is your routine tool; VACUUM FULL is a heavy hammer used when reclaiming OS space is essential and downtime is acceptable.

screens.title: Autovacuum: tuning for busy tables
screens.narratorSegment: Autovacuum is PostgreSQL’s built-in background mechanism that runs VACUUM and ANALYZE when tables meet activity thresholds. It should be enabled in production, but the defaults are not optimal for every workload. Key settings include autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor and autovacuum_vacuum_threshold, which together determine how many changed tuples trigger a vacuum: a fraction of table size plus an absolute threshold. For very large or frequently updated tables, you may want to set a lower scale factor or threshold at the table level with ALTER TABLE... SET (...) to force more frequent vacuums. Autovacuum cost settings — autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay and autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit — control how aggressive autovacuum is; reducing cost_delay makes it run faster but consumes more input and output. A practical example: for a very busy table, set autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.001 to trigger vacuums more often. A common misconception is to disable autovacuum to avoid its resource usage; this leads to accumulating bloat and XID risk. Always tune rather than disable, and monitor the autovacuum worker activity in pg_stat_activity and autovacuum logs. Closing question: what parameter would you change to make autovacuum run more frequently on a large, busy table and why?

keyIdea.title: Tune, don't disable
keyIdea.text: Adjust autovacuum thresholds and cost settings globally or per-table so vacuuming matches workload patterns without causing unnecessary disruption.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Autovacuum tuning
Key parameters
  • autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor & autovacuum_vacuum_threshold — when vacuums trigger.
  • autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor & autovacuum_analyze_threshold — when to analyze.
  • autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay & autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit — throttle autovacuum I/O.
Per-table tuning
ALTER TABLE my_busy_table
  SET (
    autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.001,
    autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = 1000
  );

Use table-level settings to ensure very active tables are vacuumed more aggressively than defaults.

Concrete example

If autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.2 on a table with 10 million rows, vacuum triggers after 2 million updates; for a busy table you may want 0.001 so vacuum runs after 10,000 updates instead.

Misconception check

Disabling autovacuum to avoid resource usage is dangerous. Tune thresholds and costs to balance I/O with bloat prevention instead of turning it off.

screens.title: Temporary files and work_mem
screens.narratorSegment: Some queries use large sorts or hash operations that require more memory than work_mem allows, and when that happens PostgreSQL writes temporary files to disk. Excessive temporary-file creation increases input and output and can slow or stall queries. You can log all temp files by setting log_temp_files to zero and then examine the logs to find problem queries. EXPLAIN ANALYZE will report "disk" or "spill" indicators which confirm a spill happened for a particular plan node. A practical remediation path is: tune work_mem upward for the session or query if the query is legitimately memory-hungry and safe to increase, or rewrite the query to reduce memory needs. A key misconception is to globally set work_mem very high without understanding concurrency: work_mem is per operation, and raising it dramatically can blow out total memory usage if many sessions run heavy queries concurrently. Example: raise work_mem in a session, re-run the query and confirm reduced temp files in logs and EXPLAIN. Closing takeaway: use targeted increases to work_mem for known heavy queries and monitor overall memory usage to avoid replacing input and output problems with out-of-memory situations.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Temporary files & work_mem
Cause

When an operation needs more memory than work_mem, PostgreSQL spills to a temp file on disk for sorts, hashes, and aggregations.

Detection
  • Enable log_temp_files = 0 to capture temp-file creation in logs.
  • Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see which plan nodes spilled to disk.
Guideline

Raise work_mem for the session or query when you know the workload and concurrency will not exhaust RAM; avoid global excessive increases.

Example steps
  1. Set log_temp_files = 0 and reproduce the query to find temp-file lines in the logs.
  2. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the query and find nodes that spill to disk.
  3. Test raising work_mem in a session and re-run the query to confirm reduced spills.
Common mistake

Increasing work_mem globally without accounting for concurrent sessions can cause excessive overall memory usage; target the session or query instead.

screens.title: Transaction ID (XID) wraparound and freezing
screens.narratorSegment: PostgreSQL assigns a 32-bit transaction ID to each transaction. Over time these IDs increase and older IDs must be frozen to avoid a wraparound that could make newer IDs conflict with older ones. The database tracks the oldest unfrozen transaction ID with datfrozenxid (per-database) and relfrozenxid (per-relation). Autovacuum is responsible for freezing old transactions before they reach autovacuum_freeze_max_age, but if autovacuum cannot keep up or is disabled, warnings appear in logs indicating databases must be vacuumed. The long-term fix is to tune autovacuum so freezes happen early enough. If warnings approach critical thresholds, run manual VACUUM FREEZE on affected tables to force freezing; be aware this is a heavy operation and requires careful planning. A common misconception is to ignore these warnings because everyday queries still succeed; however, ignoring them risks forced read-only states or data corruption. Concrete monitoring steps include querying age(datfrozenxid) from pg_database and age(relfrozenxid) from pg_class and comparing them to autovacuum_freeze_max_age. Closing question: how would you respond if age(datfrozenxid) approached the configured freeze threshold? Transaction ID (XID) wraparound and freezing means monitor age(datfrozenxid) and relfrozenxid and run vacuum freeze if autovacuum cannot keep up to avoid wraparound.. In practical terms, why age(datfrozenxid) matters and how vacuum freeze protects data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › XID wraparound
What to monitor
  • SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) FROM pg_database ORDER BY age(datfrozenxid) DESC;
  • SELECT relname, age(relfrozenxid) FROM pg_class WHERE relkind = 'r' ORDER BY age(relfrozenxid) DESC;
Autovacuum role

Autovacuum automatically freezes old XIDs. Tune autovacuum_freeze_max_age and other settings if your workload ages XIDs quickly.

Urgent action

If warnings approach the threshold, run VACUUM FREEZE on the affected tables or the whole database to prevent wraparound and possible forced read-only state.

Concrete example

If age(datfrozenxid) approaches autovacuum_freeze_max_age, increase autovacuum aggressiveness and run manual VACUUM FREEZE on critical tables as an immediate mitigation.

Misconception check

Do not ignore XID warnings because regular queries still succeed. Wraparound risk is a safety issue that must be addressed before it becomes imminent.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Hands-on lab
Lab steps overview
  1. Create a bloated table and insert many rows.
  2. Run repeated UPDATE and DELETE statements to generate dead tuples.
  3. Measure sizes and dead/live tuple counts.
  4. Run VACUUM VERBOSE, measure, then VACUUM FULL VERBOSE and measure again.
Starter SQL snippets
CREATE TABLE bloated_table (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  data TEXT DEFAULT repeat('X', 100),
  value INT
);

INSERT INTO bloated_table (value)
SELECT i FROM generate_series(1, 100000) AS i;

-- generate bloat
UPDATE bloated_table SET value = value + 1 WHERE id % 2 = 0;
DELETE FROM bloated_table WHERE id % 7 = 0;

-- measure
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('bloated_table'));
SELECT n_live_tup, n_dead_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'bloated_table';

-- reclaim
VACUUM VERBOSE bloated_table;
VACUUM FULL VERBOSE bloated_table;
What to observe
  • n_dead_tup should rise after updates/deletes and fall after VACUUM.
  • pg_total_relation_size may not fall after VACUUM, but will after VACUUM FULL.
  • Use these observations to choose routine VACUUM or schedule VACUUM FULL when necessary.
Safety note

Run the heavier VACUUM FULL only during maintenance windows because it takes an exclusive lock and can block application activity.

screens.title: Monitoring and long-term maintenance practices
screens.narratorSegment: A regular maintenance routine prevents most storage surprises. Daily checks should include monitoring free disk space and recent autovacuum activity in logs. Weekly tasks include running size reports for top relations and inspecting pg_stat_user_tables for unusually high dead-tuple counts. For emergency responses, check age(datfrozenxid) and relfrozenxid immediately and consider VACUUM FREEZE if autovacuum cannot keep up. Keep a policy: use VACUUM regularly, only use VACUUM FULL during planned windows, and reindex when index bloat is the main problem. Automate logging for temp files and capture EXPLAIN plans for slow queries so you can find spills to disk quickly. A practical misconception to avoid is treating vacuuming as a purely optional housekeeping task; in PostgreSQL it is central to correctness and performance. Include verification steps in your runbook: capture size and tuple counts before and after maintenance, and record changes. Closing reflection: with these checks in place, you will detect trends early and avoid urgent, disruptive maintenance later. Daily
  • Check disk free space and autovacuum log entries.
  • Alert on large temp-file creation events.
Weekly
  • Run the top-20 pg_total_relation_size report and inspect pg_stat_user_tables.
  • Identify candidates for reindexing, VACUUM, or VACUUM FULL.
Emergency

For each maintenance action, record pre- and post- sizes and tuple counts so you can prove effectiveness and refine thresholds over time.

fullNarratorScript:
This chapter teaches you how to find where PostgreSQL consumes disk space, why storage grows beyond live data, and how to fix it with practical maintenance. You will learn the pg_* size functions that give precise disk measurements, the causes and costs of table and index bloat, and the operational choices between VACUUM and VACUUM FULL. We'll also cover autovacuum tuning so vacuuming keeps pace with updates, how to identify costly temporary-file spill behavior tied to work_mem, and the critical problem of transaction ID wraparound and how to monitor and prevent it. By the end, you'll be able to run targeted queries to list large relations, interpret n_dead_tup and pg_total_relation_size, and choose maintenance steps that minimize downtime. A quick example: you will see how a table with heavy updates can report millions of dead tuples while still serving queries; a careful VACUUM reclaims reuse capacity while VACUUM FULL returns space to the OS but requires an exclusive lock. Think about a busy log or audit table: do you vacuum frequently to avoid massive bloat, or schedule a maintenance window for VACUUM FULL if you must release disk to the operating system? That contrast will guide many operational choices in real systems.

Over the next screens you will gain measurable skills that let you find where PostgreSQL stores data, identify waste, and take safe corrective action. First, you will be able to identify and quantify disk usage by databases, tables, and indexes using the pg_database_size, pg_relation_size and related functions. That skill helps you map storage consumption and prioritize targets. Second, you will learn to recognize table and index bloat, what causes it under MVCC, and how bloat affects input and output and cache efficiency. Third, you will become fluent with VACUUM strategies: when to run a regular VACUUM, when VACUUM FULL is appropriate, and how autovacuum settings influence system behavior. Finally, you will monitor temporary-file creation and transaction ID age to prevent performance issues and critical wraparound risks. Each objective includes small, practical checks you can run immediately, so these are not just concepts — they are operational tasks you can perform to keep production systems healthy.

These objectives add actionable steps you will be able to perform immediately. You will learn to craft queries that list the largest tables and show index versus table size so you can target work. You will practice interpreting pg_stat_user_tables fields such as n_live_tup and n_dead_tup to quantify bloat and decide whether VACUUM alone will restore reuse. You'll learn to tune autovacuum settings globally and per-table with examples like setting a lower autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor for very busy relations to force more frequent vacuums. You will also be able to diagnose excessive temporary-file creation by enabling log_temp_files and reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE for disk spills, and then adjust work_mem safely. Finally, you'll learn how to monitor transaction ID age with age(datfrozenxid) and age(relfrozenxid), and when to run VACUUM FREEZE to prevent wraparound. Each objective includes a short verification step so these are practical operational skills, not just theory.

A necessary first step in any storage problem is measurement. PostgreSQL provides a small set of functions that let you measure database, tablespace, relation, and index usage precisely. For example, pg_database_size returns the total size of a database on disk. Pg_relation_size returns the size of a table's data fork only, while pg_total_relation_size includes indexes and TOAST. Pg_indexes_size reports the combined size of all indexes for a table. These functions are safe to run and are efficient ways to focus your attention on the largest consumers. A common pattern is to query pg_class or pg_stat_user_tables and order by pg_total_relation_size to list the top space users; that is the practical starting point for most cleanup tasks. A frequent misconception is to assume that VACUUM will always reduce the number reported by pg_total_relation_size; regular VACUUM frees tuples for reuse inside the same file but does not shrink the file on disk. Only VACUUM FULL, which rewrites the table, returns space to the operating system. Table bloat arises from PostgreSQL's MVCC model where updates and deletes create new row versions and mark old ones as dead. Those dead tuples remain in the table until VACUUM marks their space reusable. If updates or deletes are frequent and vacuuming is too slow, the on-disk file grows with many dead tuples. That causes larger reads, increased input and output, slower sequential scans, and reduced cache efficiency. An example: a table with one million live rows but five million dead tuples will require scanning many pages containing dead data, harming performance and increasing storage usage. Important nuance: a regular VACUUM reclaims space for reuse inside the table file so future inserts can use that free space, but it does not shrink the file visible to the operating system. VACUUM FULL rewrites the table to a smaller file and returns the freed space to the OS, but it locks the table and is therefore a maintenance-window operation. A common misconception is to equate a lower n_dead_tup with no bloat; sometimes n_dead_tup can be reset by VACUUM while the file remains large because vacuum did not shrink the file. Closing takeaway: measure live and dead tuples, decide whether reuse or OS-level shrinkage is the goal, and then choose VACUUM or VACUUM FULL accordingly.

Index bloat occurs when indexed columns are frequently updated, and the index retains dead entries that are no longer needed. For B-tree indexes, this increases tree height and page count and leads to larger index scans and more random input and output. Index bloat may be less visible in pg_relation_size because index space is reported separately, but pg_indexes_size and pg_total_relation_size will reveal large index footprints. A concrete example is a heavily updated timestamp column that is part of many indexes; repeated updates generate dead index entries that remain until reindexing or maintenance collapses them. Misconceptions include thinking that VACUUM always fixes index bloat; while VACUUM can clean some index entries, heavy index bloat often requires REINDEX or even index drop-and-recreate to reclaim space effectively. When inspecting a large index, consider whether the index is needed or whether it can be rebuilt during a maintenance window. Key takeaway: treat index bloat separately from table bloat and choose reindexing if index pages are the primary consumer of disk and performance is suffering. Deciding between VACUUM and VACUUM FULL is a matter of goals and availability. VACUUM reclaims space occupied by dead tuples and marks it for reuse within the same table file. It is safe to run concurrently and typically should be the first step to reduce n_dead_tup and improve future operations. VACUUM FULL rewrites the table and its indexes to new files, physically shrinking the on-disk footprint and returning space to the operating system; however, it requires an exclusive lock and can block concurrent access, so schedule it during a maintenance window. A safe operational flow is: 1) Measure sizes and dead tuples; 2) Run VACUUM to reclaim reuse space and reduce dead tuple counts; 3) If you must return space to the OS for capacity reasons, plan VACUUM FULL during a quiet period and inform stakeholders. Misconception: running VACUUM FULL repeatedly without addressing root causes such as high update churn or insufficient autovacuum will only delay recurrence. Example commands shown here include VACUUM VERBOSE my_table and VACUUM FULL VERBOSE my_table. Closing question: for a busy audit table with five times more dead tuples than live tuples, which vacuum do you run first and why?

Autovacuum is PostgreSQL’s built-in background mechanism that runs VACUUM and ANALYZE when tables meet activity thresholds. It should be enabled in production, but the defaults are not optimal for every workload. Key settings include autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor and autovacuum_vacuum_threshold, which together determine how many changed tuples trigger a vacuum: a fraction of table size plus an absolute threshold. For very large or frequently updated tables, you may want to set a lower scale factor or threshold at the table level with ALTER TABLE... SET (...) to force more frequent vacuums. Autovacuum cost settings — autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay and autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit — control how aggressive autovacuum is; reducing cost_delay makes it run faster but consumes more input and output. A practical example: for a very busy table, set autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.001 to trigger vacuums more often. A common misconception is to disable autovacuum to avoid its resource usage; this leads to accumulating bloat and XID risk. Always tune rather than disable, and monitor the autovacuum worker activity in pg_stat_activity and autovacuum logs. Closing question: what parameter would you change to make autovacuum run more frequently on a large, busy table and why?

Some queries use large sorts or hash operations that require more memory than work_mem allows, and when that happens PostgreSQL writes temporary files to disk. Excessive temporary-file creation increases input and output and can slow or stall queries. You can log all temp files by setting log_temp_files to zero and then examine the logs to find problem queries. EXPLAIN ANALYZE will report "disk" or "spill" indicators which confirm a spill happened for a particular plan node. A practical remediation path is: tune work_mem upward for the session or query if the query is legitimately memory-hungry and safe to increase, or rewrite the query to reduce memory needs. A key misconception is to globally set work_mem very high without understanding concurrency: work_mem is per operation, and raising it dramatically can blow out total memory usage if many sessions run heavy queries concurrently. Example: raise work_mem in a session, re-run the query and confirm reduced temp files in logs and EXPLAIN. Closing takeaway: use targeted increases to work_mem for known heavy queries and monitor overall memory usage to avoid replacing input and output problems with out-of-memory situations.

PostgreSQL assigns a 32-bit transaction ID to each transaction. Over time these IDs increase and older IDs must be frozen to avoid a wraparound that could make newer IDs conflict with older ones. The database tracks the oldest unfrozen transaction ID with datfrozenxid (per-database) and relfrozenxid (per-relation). Autovacuum is responsible for freezing old transactions before they reach autovacuum_freeze_max_age, but if autovacuum cannot keep up or is disabled, warnings appear in logs indicating databases must be vacuumed. The long-term fix is to tune autovacuum so freezes happen early enough. If warnings approach critical thresholds, run manual VACUUM FREEZE on affected tables to force freezing; be aware this is a heavy operation and requires careful planning. A common misconception is to ignore these warnings because everyday queries still succeed; however, ignoring them risks forced read-only states or data corruption. Concrete monitoring steps include querying age(datfrozenxid) from pg_database and age(relfrozenxid) from pg_class and comparing them to autovacuum_freeze_max_age. A regular maintenance routine prevents most storage surprises. Daily checks should include monitoring free disk space and recent autovacuum activity in logs. Weekly tasks include running size reports for top relations and inspecting pg_stat_user_tables for unusually high dead-tuple counts. For emergency responses, check age(datfrozenxid) and relfrozenxid immediately and consider VACUUM FREEZE if autovacuum cannot keep up. Keep a policy: use VACUUM regularly, only use VACUUM FULL during planned windows, and reindex when index bloat is the main problem. Automate logging for temp files and capture EXPLAIN plans for slow queries so you can find spills to disk quickly. A practical misconception to avoid is treating vacuuming as a purely optional housekeeping task; in PostgreSQL it is central to correctness and performance. Include verification steps in your runbook: capture size and tuple counts before and after maintenance, and record changes. Here are the core ideas to carry forward. First, measure before acting: use pg_relation_size and pg_total_relation_size to find real disk consumers. Second, bloat comes from MVCC dead tuples and index dead entries; VACUUM reclaims space for reuse while VACUUM FULL rewrites files and returns space to the operating system. Third, autovacuum must be tuned to match workload; per-table settings can force more frequent vacuums on busy relations. These three principles — measure, diagnose, and apply the least-invasive fix — form the backbone of storage maintenance.
